doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Learning to read from the red notes in Chico's piano part
summary: The red-ink trumpet lines in piano/conductor parts taught him to read; he joined Chico in February 1942.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: with comedians and dancers, I was lucky that we had an 18 piece orchestra. And fortunately I had what they called a piano/conductor part. And on the top, in red ink, was what the lead trumpet was playing, see? So now I would fake through the first show and from the second show on I would follow the red notes on the piano sheets see? And I would notice like whenever the band had an eighth rest and a dotted quarter, I know it always went [scats] and I said, hey that’s great, you know. By the time I left that band I was reading music.
That’s fascinating. And that must have been standard procedure for those arrangers back then to put the trumpet part in red?

Well no it wasn’t that, it was the people who had the act, like the dance team or the comedian or the harmonica player, whoever, they would hand out their parts. It wasn’t the orchestra parts, it was the parts from the act that we were playing.

Because when they didn’t know they would say well this is the drummer’s part, and this is the saxophone players, and this is the piano/conductor, because the piano player was usually the conductor. And they would say piano/conductor. So I was lucky because all of those things had those red lines, those red music dots on there, and that’s how I learned how to read. In fact the funny thing was, only about three years ago, my wife and I were sitting in the living room and I said, “well you know I scuffled during Chico’s band because I couldn’t read.” She said, “you didn’t know how to read when you were with Chico’s band?” She never even knew I couldn’t read. Because we were too busy, we had just gotten married, we were busy doing something else.
1942, February. I joined them February of ’42.
